name: PsiTri (arbtrie)
workload: TATP-style bank-transfer benchmark: 1,000,000 accounts, 10,000,000 transfer attempts, 5 KV ops per atomic transaction (2 reads, 2 updates, 1 insert)
claimed_speedup: PsiTriRocks (RocksDB-compatible drop-in API) vs RocksDB: 2.3x write speedup, 4.9x read speedup (April 2026, AMD EPYC-Turin). PsiTri itself vs RocksDB in the same bank benchmark: 376,691 vs 126,341 transfers/sec (~2.98x, derived from page data) on Apple M5 Max; 163,614 vs 104,102 transfers/sec (~1.57x, derived from page data) on AMD EPYC-Turin
compiler_and_flags: Apple M5 Max: Clang 17, C++20, -O3 -flto=thin. AMD EPYC-Turin: Clang 20, C++20, -O3 -flto -march=native (AVX-512 enabled)
hardware: Apple M5 Max (ARM64, macOS); AMD EPYC-Turin (x86-64, Linux)
tradeoffs: Also ships PsiTri-SQLite (SQLite drop-in) claiming 1.06x write / 13.5x read vs SQLite in the same bank benchmark, and separately 47x (sync=off) / 3.8x (sync=full) on a TATP telecom benchmark without hardware stated for that specific table. Very new project; README/repo name mismatch (repo is 'arbtrie', product now called 'PsiTri') suggests a recent rename/pivot, so API and durability guarantees may still be in flux.
caveats: Only 4 GitHub stars despite strong numbers, so there is no independent replication yet. MDBX beat PsiTri outright on the AMD EPYC machine in the same table (239,041 vs 163,614 transfers/sec), so the win over RocksDB does not extend to a win over every incumbent tested.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/gofractally/arbtrie/readme (found via gh search code "faster than RocksDB"-style crawl of embedded-kv repos), confirmed at https://gofractally.github.io/arbtrie/benchmarks/bank/

name: SpanDB
workload: LSM-tree KV store evaluation on hybrid NVMe+SSD storage, YCSB-derived workloads comparing SpanDB against unmodified RocksDB via the repo's bundled `test` harness (dbname=rocksdb|spandb)
claimed_speedup: "improves RocksDB's throughput by up to 8.8x" and "reduces its latency by 9.5-58.3%" (quoted from the USENIX FAST'21 paper page)
tradeoffs: Requires SPDK plus manual NVMe setup (hugepages, unbinding devices from the kernel driver), a much heavier deployment than plain RocksDB. Built by adapting the RocksDB codebase (not flagged as a GitHub fork, but derived from it) to place WAL and top LSM levels on faster NVMe.
caveats: Numbers taken from the peer-reviewed paper's abstract page, not independently re-verified in this session; the full PDF (which likely states hardware/compiler) was not opened. Repo has had no commits since August 2023, i.e. an unmaintained research prototype.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "LSM tree" "faster" language:c++ --sort stars

name: ToplingDB
workload: db_bench fillrandom/readrandom suite, 50,000,000 records, 8-byte keys, 50-byte values, ~1.9 GiB dataset that fits inside the 7.8 GiB block cache
claimed_speedup: readrandom: ToplingDB zipkeyonly 4,720,755 ops/sec vs RocksDB v8.10 348,705 ops/sec (~13.5x, derived from page data) and vs RocksDB master 378,000 ops/sec; ToplingDB zipkeyvalue quoted on-page as '18% memory / 4.98x speed' vs RocksDB v8.10
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor (4 logical CPUs allotted), Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, 15.6 GiB RAM
tradeoffs: GPL-2.0 is more restrictive than RocksDB's BSD/Apache-2.0 dual license, which can block adoption in permissively-licensed downstream projects. Several advertised features (distributed compaction, some CSPP tooling) are gated behind a separate paid 'Enterprise' build not in this open repo.
caveats: Benchmark is run and published by the ToplingDB project itself (not an independent third party); the results page states hardware and dataset but not the compiler or build flags used. The tested dataset is fully cache-resident, which favors ToplingDB's read-path/de-virtualization optimizations and may not generalize to larger-than-cache workloads.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos --topic embedded-database --sort stars

name: CalicoDB
workload: db_bench-style micro-benchmark suite (fillseq, fillrandom, readrandom, readseq, fillrand100K, readrand100K, etc.) run in CI on GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest and macos-latest runners, CalicoDB 0.0.1 vs SQLite3 3.39.5
claimed_speedup: readrand100K: 58.801 microsec/op vs SQLite3's 252.367 microsec/op on Linux (~4.3x, derived from page data); 79.160 vs 495.537 microsec/op on macOS (~6.3x, derived from page data). Mixed on other workloads: CalicoDB is slower than SQLite3 on fillrandom, overwrite, and fillrandbatch
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest / macos-latest runners (exact CPU model unstated)
tradeoffs: Results are mixed rather than a clean win: faster on sequential writes and large random-read batches, slower on plain random writes/overwrites. Tiny, low-visibility project (43 stars).
caveats: Benchmarked on generic CI runners (no fixed CPU model) with no stated compiler flags, so it falls short of Tier A despite public benchmark code. No commits since November 2023.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos --topic key-value-store language:cpp --sort stars

name: UStore (UDisk engine)
workload: 1 TB binary KV workload (scan, batch read, read, read+update, read+upsert, batch upsert, remove) via the companion UCSB benchmark harness, UDisk vs RocksDB
claimed_speedup: As of December 2022 (quoted table): Batch Read 650K -> 4.5M ops/sec (~6.9x, derived from page data); Batch Upsert 57K -> 260K ops/sec (~4.6x, derived); Remove 420K -> 874K ops/sec (~2.1x, derived); Read&Update 1:1 64K -> 173K ops/sec (~2.7x, derived)
tradeoffs: UDisk is Unum's own default embedded engine inside UStore (distinct from the pure in-memory UCSet backend); the companion low-level harness, unum-cloud/ucsb, also benchmarks LMDB, LevelDB, and WiredTiger natively but that harness repo carries no license (license: null), so treat it as reference-only even though UStore itself is Apache-2.0.
caveats: Table is explicitly labeled 'typical results ... as of December 2022' with no hardware or compiler stated in that table; last commit to UStore's default branch was 2023-08-18 despite more recent pushes to other branches, so treat the whole project as unmaintained.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos --topic key-value-store language:cpp --sort stars, then repo file listing at benchmarks/README.md

name: Speedb
workload: Massive random-write workload: 80,000,000 objects, 1 KB value size, 50 threads
claimed_speedup: README graph shows Speedb sustaining consistent write throughput without stalling versus RocksDB under the stated write workload; no exact numeric ratio is given in text, only a chart image
tradeoffs: 100% RocksDB-API-compatible drop-in, so switching cost for existing RocksDB users is near zero.
caveats: Only a chart image backs the claim; no quoted throughput numbers, hardware, or compiler flags are given in the README. Included as the one permitted Tier D entry given its scale (1009 stars). Commit activity has slowed sharply since early 2024.
